COVER MEMORANDUM
June 1, 2026
TO: Zava Legal — Technology Transactions Group; Procurement Department; Information Security Office; Product & AI Strategy (Hemanti Baishya, VP); Business-Unit Stakeholders including Chief Underwriting Officer (Luc Lacombe) and their respective teams
FROM: Emil Vanggaard, Associate General Counsel — Technology Transactions
RE: AI Procurement Playbook v.2.1 — Mandatory Standards for AI/ML Vendor Agreement Evaluation, Negotiation, and Execution
The purpose of this Playbook is to establish Zava, Inc.'s ("Zava" or the "Company") mandatory standards, required contractual positions, acceptable fallback positions, risk ratings, and escalation thresholds for the evaluation, negotiation, and execution of all agreements with third-party vendors providing artificial intelligence and machine learning products and services (collectively, "AI/ML vendors"). This Playbook is designed to be a comprehensive, actionable reference that equips each member of the Zava deal team — whether from Legal, Procurement, Information Security, Product & AI Strategy, or a business unit — with the tools and authority framework necessary to protect the Company's interests throughout the AI vendor procurement lifecycle.
This Playbook is addressed to and intended for the following audiences:
•  Zava Legal — Technology Transactions Group: As the primary negotiators and drafters of AI vendor agreements, the Technology Transactions team is responsible for ensuring that every agreement conforms to the positions set forth herein or that any deviation is properly escalated and documented.
•  Procurement Department: Procurement personnel are responsible for initial vendor sourcing, RFP processes, and commercial-term negotiations. This Playbook provides the guardrails within which Procurement may operate and identifies the escalation points at which Legal must be engaged.
•  Information Security Office: The InfoSec team is responsible for evaluating vendor security posture, reviewing SOC 2 reports and penetration-test results, and advising on data-protection and incident-response provisions. The security and audit requirements in Sections 3 and 4 of this Playbook reflect InfoSec's minimum requirements.
•  Product & AI Strategy (Hemanti Baishya, VP): As the executive sponsor for Zava's AI strategy, the VP of Product & AI Strategy serves as a required approver for certain high-value and high-risk deviations and is responsible for evaluating model-governance and portability provisions from a strategic perspective.
•  Business-Unit Stakeholders, including Chief Underwriting Officer (Luc Lacombe) and their teams: Business-unit leaders who sponsor or consume AI vendor solutions must understand the contractual framework within which those solutions will operate. The underwriting function, in particular, is directly affected by model-governance, bias-testing, explainability, and change-control provisions, given the regulatory scrutiny applied to AI-assisted insurance decisioning.
Supersession. This Playbook (v.2.1) supersedes the AI Procurement Playbook v.2.0, dated November 24, 2025, and all prior internal guidance, memoranda, checklists, and informal protocols relating to the procurement of AI/ML vendor products and services. To the extent any prior guidance conflicts with this Playbook, this Playbook controls. All deal-team members should discard or archive prior versions and rely solely on this document going forward.
Applicability. This Playbook applies to all AI/ML vendor agreements regardless of contract value, including but not limited to master services agreements, statements of work, order forms, pilot and proof-of-concept agreements, amendments, renewals, and extensions. However, the escalation and approval requirements set forth herein are tiered by Annual Contract Value (ACV) bands as detailed in the Decision Matrix (Section 13). This tiered approach ensures that the level of scrutiny and seniority of approval are proportionate to the financial and operational risk of each engagement.
Risk Context. Zava's AI deployments are, by their nature, high-risk. The Company's core use of third-party AI/ML platforms is in regulated insurance decisioning, particularly underwriting. AI-assisted underwriting decisions directly affect policyholders and are subject to increasing regulatory scrutiny at both the state and federal levels. The Colorado Division of Insurance has issued specific guidance on the use of AI in insurance, the New York Department of Financial Services has signaled heightened enforcement priorities in this area, and the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) continues to develop model bulletins addressing AI governance. Any failure in an AI vendor's model — whether due to bias, data-quality deficiencies, unexplained decisioning, or unauthorized model changes — could expose Zava to regulatory enforcement actions, litigation, reputational harm, and financial loss. The contractual protections set forth in this Playbook are calibrated to this risk profile.
EU Market Expansion. Zava's expansion into EU markets introduces a significant additional regulatory overlay. Every AI vendor agreement must now be evaluated for compliance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), including the requirement for GDPR-compliant Data Processing Agreements, and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act), which imposes specific obligations on deployers and providers of high-risk AI systems. The insurance sector is explicitly identified as a high-risk domain under the EU AI Act. Sections 3 and 9 of this Playbook address these requirements in detail, and negotiators must ensure that every AI vendor agreement includes the necessary provisions to support Zava's EU operations.
Playbook Owner. Emil Vanggaard, Associate General Counsel — Technology Transactions, is the designated owner of this Playbook. All questions regarding interpretation, all requests for exceptions, and all escalation decisions that are not otherwise addressed by the Decision Matrix should be directed to Emil Vanggaard. Emil Vanggaard has the authority to approve exceptions to any non-hard-stop provision of this Playbook, subject to the escalation requirements set forth in Section 13 for high-ACV engagements.
All Zava personnel involved in AI vendor procurement are expected to familiarize themselves with this Playbook in its entirety and to consult it at each stage of the procurement process. Compliance with this Playbook is mandatory, not aspirational.
SECTION 1 — SCOPE & DEFINITIONS
1.1 Scope.  This Playbook governs all agreements entered into by Zava, Inc. with vendors that provide artificial intelligence or machine learning models, platforms, application programming interfaces (APIs), or related services to the Company. The scope of this Playbook is intentionally broad and encompasses the following agreement types without limitation:
•  Master Services Agreements (MSAs): Overarching agreements establishing the general terms and conditions governing the vendor relationship.
•  Statements of Work (SOWs): Individual project- or service-specific work orders issued under an MSA or on a standalone basis.
•  Order Forms: Commercial documents specifying quantities, pricing, term, and other transactional details for specific products or services.
•  Pilot and Proof-of-Concept (POC) Agreements: Limited-scope, time-bound agreements entered into for evaluation purposes. Notwithstanding their preliminary nature, pilot and POC agreements frequently involve the processing of Company Data and must include appropriate data-protection and IP provisions.
•  Amendments and Renewals: Modifications to existing agreements, including term extensions, scope expansions, and pricing adjustments. All amendments and renewals must be evaluated against the current version of this Playbook, not the version in effect at the time of the original agreement.
•  Licensing Agreements: Agreements for the licensing of AI/ML models, algorithms, or software components on a standalone basis.
•  Data-as-a-Service Agreements: Agreements under which a vendor provides data sets, data feeds, or data enrichment services that serve as inputs to AI/ML models or platforms.
This Playbook covers both SaaS-delivered AI/ML solutions (where the vendor hosts and operates the platform in its own or a third-party cloud environment) and on-premises or hybrid deployments (where all or a portion of the AI/ML platform is deployed within Zava's own infrastructure or a Zava-controlled cloud environment). The deployment model affects certain provisions — particularly those related to security, audit rights, and data residency — but the core IP, data-ownership, liability, and governance requirements apply regardless of deployment architecture.
This Playbook applies regardless of whether the agreement is documented on the vendor's standard form or on Zava's own paper. When negotiating on a vendor's form, the Technology Transactions team must systematically mark up the vendor's form to conform to the Required Positions set forth herein, or document approved Fallback Positions in the negotiation tracker. When using Zava's own form, the Technology Transactions team must verify that the form incorporates all Required Positions and has been updated to reflect the current version of this Playbook.
1.2 Defined Terms
The following defined terms are used throughout this Playbook and should be incorporated, as applicable, into each AI vendor agreement. Where a vendor's form uses different terminology for substantially similar concepts, the Technology Transactions team should map the vendor's defined terms to the Playbook definitions and ensure substantive equivalence.
"ACV" (Annual Contract Value) means the Total Contract Value divided by the number of years in the initial term of the agreement. For purposes of clarity, if an agreement has a Total Contract Value of $14,750,000 over a five-year initial term, the ACV is $2,950,000. ACV is used as the primary metric for determining escalation thresholds under the Decision Matrix (Section 13) and for calculating liability-cap benchmarks (Section 5).
"Company" means Zava, Inc., a Delaware corporation, together with its subsidiaries and affiliates to the extent designated in the applicable agreement.
"Company Data" means all data provided by or on behalf of Company to Vendor in connection with the agreement, all data generated by Company's use of the Platform (including usage data, configuration data, and metadata), and all derivatives, inferences, embeddings, vectors, and outputs produced by the Platform using Company Data as input. For the avoidance of doubt, Company Data includes policyholder data, underwriting data, claims data, actuarial data, and any other data originating from Company's operations or provided by Company's customers, partners, or agents.
"Fine-Tuned Model Weights" means the parameter values of any machine-learning model that have been adjusted, retrained, fine-tuned, or otherwise modified using Company Data, including any adapter layers, LoRA weights, or similar parameter-efficient fine-tuning artifacts. Fine-Tuned Model Weights are distinct from Vendor's base model weights and pre-existing IP.
"Material Model Change" means any modification to a model deployed in connection with Company's use of the Platform that results in greater than two percent (2%) variance in output distribution (as measured against a representative validation data set agreed between the parties), or any change to the sources of training data used in such models. Material Model Changes include, without limitation, retraining on new data sets, architecture modifications, hyperparameter changes that exceed the defined variance threshold, and substitution of one model for another.
"Model Card" means a structured document describing a model's intended use, out-of-scope uses, performance metrics (including accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and AUC as applicable), training data characteristics and provenance, known limitations, bias and fairness evaluation results, and version history. Model Cards should be consistent with the guidance published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) under the AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) and reflect industry best practices.
"Outputs/Inferences" means all results, predictions, scores, risk assessments, recommendations, classifications, rankings, embeddings, or other outputs generated by the Platform in response to Company Data inputs, whether generated in real time, batch mode, or any other processing mode.
"Platform" means the AI/ML software, models, algorithms, APIs, dashboards, user interfaces, and supporting infrastructure provided by Vendor under the agreement, including all updates, upgrades, patches, and new versions made available to Company during the term.
"Vendor" means the third-party AI/ML vendor counterparty to the agreement.
"TCV" (Total Contract Value) means the aggregate of all fees payable by Company under the agreement over the full initial term, including implementation fees, platform fees, subscription fees, and any fixed recurring fees. TCV excludes variable overage fees, professional-services fees incurred on a time-and-materials basis, and expenses, unless such fees are reasonably estimable at the time of execution, in which case they should be included in the TCV calculation for purposes of ACV-band classification.
1.3 Playbook Structure — How to Use This Document
Each substantive section of this Playbook (Sections 2 through 12) addresses a specific category of contractual terms and is organized into three tiers, as described below. This three-tier structure is designed to give negotiators clear direction while preserving the flexibility to reach commercially reasonable outcomes.
Required Position. The Required Position is the mandatory contractual position that Zava must obtain in every AI vendor agreement. The Required Position reflects the Company's optimal risk posture and aligns with regulatory requirements, industry best practices, and Zava's strategic objectives. Negotiators should present the Required Position as Zava's initial and preferred position and should not concede the Required Position without first exhausting good-faith negotiation efforts. Any deviation from a Required Position — including acceptance of a Fallback Position — must be escalated in accordance with the Decision Matrix (Section 13).
Fallback Position. The Fallback Position is an acceptable alternative that the Technology Transactions team may accept if the Required Position is rejected by the vendor after good-faith negotiation. The Fallback Position represents the minimum level of contractual protection that Zava can accept for the relevant issue without exposing the Company to undue risk. Acceptance of a Fallback Position must be documented in the negotiation tracker (Appendix E) with a brief risk-justification narrative explaining the commercial rationale for the concession and any mitigating factors. Certain issues do not have a Fallback Position because they are designated as hard stops — positions that may not be conceded under any circumstance (see Section 14).
Risk Rating for Deviation. Each material issue addressed in this Playbook is assigned a risk rating on a four-level scale:
•  Critical: Deviation from the Required Position on a Critical-rated issue creates a material risk of regulatory non-compliance, significant financial exposure, operational disruption, or loss of essential contractual protections. Critical deviations require approval from the Associate General Counsel (Emil Vanggaard). For engagements with ACV exceeding $2,000,000, Critical deviations additionally require sign-off from the VP of Product & AI Strategy (Hemanti Baishya). For engagements with ACV exceeding $5,000,000, Critical deviations require General Counsel, VP of Product & AI Strategy, and CFO approval.
•  High: Deviation from the Required Position on a High-rated issue creates a meaningful risk that, while manageable, warrants senior review. High deviations require Associate General Counsel approval for engagements with ACV of $500,000 or more and Senior Associate approval for lower-value engagements. For engagements with ACV exceeding $5,000,000, High deviations require the same approval chain as Critical deviations.
•  Medium: Deviation from the Required Position on a Medium-rated issue creates a moderate risk that can typically be mitigated through other contractual provisions or operational controls. Medium deviations may be approved by the lead Technology Transactions attorney on the deal, with documentation in the negotiation tracker.
•  Low: Deviation from the Required Position on a Low-rated issue creates a minimal incremental risk. Low deviations may be approved by the lead Technology Transactions attorney on the deal without further escalation, but should still be documented for completeness.
Throughout this Playbook, items highlighted in red or designated with the notation [HARD STOP] denote positions that may not be conceded under any circumstance, regardless of ACV band, commercial pressure, or executive direction. Hard stops are consolidated in Section 14 for ease of reference. If a vendor refuses to accept all hard-stop positions, the deal team must escalate to the General Counsel for a proceed/no-proceed determination before continuing negotiations.
Negotiators are expected to use this Playbook in conjunction with the Negotiation Tracker Template (Appendix E), which provides a structured format for documenting all deviations from Required Positions, the corresponding risk justifications, and the approvals obtained. The completed negotiation tracker must be retained in the matter file for each AI vendor engagement.
SECTION 2 — INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY & DATA OWNERSHIP
Intellectual property and data ownership provisions are the foundation of Zava's AI vendor agreements. The positions set forth in this Section are informed by the Company's strategic priority of maintaining full portability — the ability to transition away from any single AI vendor without losing the value created through the Company's investment of data, time, and resources. This priority is particularly acute given the nascent and rapidly evolving nature of the AI vendor market, where vendor consolidation, pivots, and failures are foreseeable risks.
2.1 Fine-Tuned Model Weights
Required Position: Company shall own, or at minimum co-own with full rights of independent exploitation (meaning each co-owner may use, license, and exploit the co-owned Fine-Tuned Model Weights without the consent of or accounting to the other co-owner), all Fine-Tuned Model Weights created using Company Data. Vendor must deliver all Fine-Tuned Model Weights in an industry-standard, portable format (such as ONNX, HDF5, or PyTorch-native format) upon Company's request at any time during the term and upon expiration or termination of the agreement. Delivery must be completed within thirty (30) calendar days of the request.
The rationale for this position is straightforward: Fine-Tuned Model Weights represent the incremental value created by the application of Company Data to Vendor's base models. Without ownership or co-ownership of these weights, Company would be unable to port its customized AI capabilities to a successor platform in the event of vendor transition, creating a significant lock-in risk. This is Business Priority #1 for vendor portability, as identified by the VP of Product & AI Strategy.
Fallback Position: If outright ownership or co-ownership with full rights of independent exploitation is unattainable after good-faith negotiation, Company will accept a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free, fully paid-up license to the Fine-Tuned Model Weights that is exclusive within Company's industry vertical (insurance and financial services), with the right to port, deploy, modify, and use such weights on any successor platform or internal infrastructure. The license must survive expiration or termination of the agreement for any reason. Vendor must still deliver the Fine-Tuned Model Weights in a portable format upon request or termination.
Risk Rating: Critical. Ownership of Fine-Tuned Model Weights is Business Priority #1 for vendor portability. Any deviation from the Required Position requires joint approval by Emil Vanggaard and Hemanti Baishya. Negotiators should be prepared to walk away from a deal if neither the Required Position nor the Fallback Position can be achieved. If a vendor categorically refuses to address Fine-Tuned Model Weight ownership or licensing, escalate immediately to Emil Vanggaard.
2.2 Outputs and Inferences
Required Position: All Outputs/Inferences generated by the Platform in response to Company Data inputs are the sole and exclusive property of Company. Vendor receives no rights in Outputs/Inferences — whether ownership, license, or otherwise — except as strictly necessary for Vendor to perform the services under the agreement during the term. Upon expiration or termination of the agreement, all Vendor rights in Outputs/Inferences cease immediately. Vendor shall not retain, use, analyze, aggregate, de-identify, or otherwise process Outputs/Inferences for any purpose other than performance of the services.
Fallback Position: None. [HARD STOP] No deviation is permitted from this position under any circumstance. Outputs and Inferences are the direct product of Company's proprietary data and business processes. Any grant of rights to Vendor in Outputs/Inferences would compromise Company's competitive position, create regulatory risk (particularly with respect to policyholder data), and undermine the fundamental value proposition of the vendor engagement.
Risk Rating: Critical.
2.3 Vendor Use of Company Data for Cross-Customer Model Improvement
Required Position: Vendor may not use Company Data to train, improve, fine-tune, benchmark, evaluate, or otherwise enhance models for the benefit of other Vendor customers or Vendor's general-purpose models without Company's prior written, opt-in consent for each specific use case. Generic consent clauses embedded in vendor standard forms (such as "Vendor may use Customer Data to improve the Service") are not acceptable and must be deleted or replaced with the opt-in consent mechanism described herein. Company's consent, if granted, may be revoked at any time upon written notice, and Vendor must promptly cease the consented use and certify cessation within ten (10) business days.
This position is essential for several reasons. First, Company Data includes highly sensitive policyholder and underwriting data that, even in aggregated or de-identified form, could provide competitive intelligence to other insurers or financial-services companies that use Vendor's platform. Second, regulatory frameworks — including CCPA/CPRA, GDPR, and emerging state AI governance laws — increasingly restrict secondary uses of personal data, and the use of Company Data for cross-customer model training may implicate those restrictions. Third, permitting unrestricted use of Company Data for model improvement dilutes the competitive advantage Company derives from its unique data assets.
Fallback Position: Vendor may use only fully de-identified, aggregated statistical metadata (not raw Company Data, and not individual-level or record-level data in any form) for general model improvement, subject to the following conditions: (a) Company retains the right to opt out of such use at any time upon written notice; (b) Vendor must certify the de-identification methodology used, and such methodology must satisfy the standards of the HIPAA Safe Harbor method (even if HIPAA does not directly apply) or an equivalent statistical de-identification standard; (c) Vendor must not reverse-engineer, re-identify, or attempt to re-identify any data derived from Company Data; and (d) Vendor's use of aggregated metadata must not include any data that, alone or in combination, could identify Company as the source.
Risk Rating: Critical.
2.4 Pre-Existing and Background IP
Required Position: Vendor retains ownership of its pre-existing intellectual property, including its base models, algorithms, frameworks, and proprietary tools that existed prior to the agreement or that are developed independently of Company Data ("Pre-Existing IP"). Company acknowledges Vendor's ownership of Pre-Existing IP. However, Company receives a perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free, fully paid-up, worldwide, non-exclusive license to use Vendor's Pre-Existing IP solely to the extent such Pre-Existing IP is embedded in, incorporated into, or necessary to exploit the Fine-Tuned Model Weights and Outputs/Inferences owned by or licensed to Company. This license must survive expiration or termination of the agreement.
The purpose of this provision is to ensure that Company's ownership or license of Fine-Tuned Model Weights is not rendered meaningless by Vendor's retention of rights in the underlying infrastructure necessary to use those weights. Without a perpetual license to embedded Pre-Existing IP, Company would be unable to deploy its Fine-Tuned Model Weights on a successor platform, effectively recreating the lock-in scenario that Section 2.1 is designed to prevent.
Fallback Position: The license to Pre-Existing IP may be coterminous with the agreement (i.e., it expires upon termination) only if the Fine-Tuned Model Weights ownership or license obtained under Section 2.1 provides sufficient portability without reliance on Vendor's Pre-Existing IP. This determination must be made in consultation with the VP of Product & AI Strategy or a designated technical lead, who must confirm in writing that the Fine-Tuned Model Weights can be independently deployed on commercially available successor platforms without requiring Vendor's Pre-Existing IP. If such confirmation cannot be obtained, the perpetual license is required.
Risk Rating: High.
SECTION 3 — DATA PROTECTION & PRIVACY
Data protection and privacy are areas of acute and growing regulatory risk for Zava, particularly given the Company's use of AI in regulated insurance decisioning and its expansion into EU markets. The provisions in this Section are designed to ensure that every AI vendor agreement includes robust protections that satisfy the Company's obligations under applicable data-protection and privacy laws, as well as emerging AI-specific regulations.
3.1 Applicable Privacy Laws
Required Position: Vendor must comply with all applicable data-protection and privacy laws in connection with its processing of Company Data under the agreement. At a minimum, Vendor must represent and warrant compliance with the following:
•  California Consumer Privacy Act / California Privacy Rights Act (CCPA/CPRA): Vendor must act as a "service provider" (as defined under CCPA/CPRA) with respect to personal information contained in Company Data and must contractually commit to the service-provider obligations set forth in the statute, including the prohibition on selling or sharing personal information and the restriction on use of personal information for purposes other than the business purpose specified in the agreement.
•  General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR): To the extent Company processes data of EU-resident individuals through the Platform, Vendor must act as a "processor" (as defined under GDPR) and must execute a GDPR-compliant Data Processing Agreement (DPA) as an addendum to the agreement. The DPA must include all mandatory provisions of Article 28 GDPR, including purpose limitation, sub-processor controls, data-subject-rights cooperation, and data-breach notification. This requirement is now mandatory for all AI vendor agreements, given Zava's EU market expansion.
•  Colorado Privacy Act (CPA): Vendor must comply with the CPA's requirements applicable to processors, including the duty to assist Company in meeting its obligations regarding consumer rights and data-protection assessments. The CPA is particularly relevant given Colorado's early adoption of AI-specific insurance-regulation guidance.
•  EU Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act): Vendor must comply with the EU AI Act's requirements applicable to providers of AI systems, including obligations relating to high-risk AI systems (which include AI systems used in the insurance sector for risk assessment and pricing). Vendor must cooperate with Company in meeting Company's obligations as a "deployer" of high-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act, including record-keeping, transparency, and human oversight requirements.
Vendor must represent and warrant ongoing compliance with all of the foregoing laws and must promptly notify Company — in no event later than ten (10) business days after becoming aware — of any change in its compliance status, any regulatory inquiry or enforcement action relating to its data-processing or AI practices, or any material change in law that could affect its ability to perform the services in compliance with applicable law.
Fallback Position: If Vendor cannot represent full GDPR compliance at the time of agreement execution (for example, because Vendor is in the process of obtaining necessary certifications or implementing required technical measures), Vendor must achieve compliance within ninety (90) days of the Effective Date and must execute a GDPR-compliant DPA as a condition precedent to any processing of EU-resident data. During the interim period, Company shall not process any EU-resident data through the Platform, and the agreement must include a contractual mechanism to prevent such processing until GDPR compliance is confirmed.
Risk Rating: Critical for CCPA/CPRA and GDPR compliance; High for CPA and EU AI Act compliance.
3.2 Algorithmic Audits
Required Position: Company has the right to conduct, or to commission an independent, qualified third party to conduct, an algorithmic audit of the Platform at least once per year. The scope of the audit shall include, at a minimum: (a) evaluation of the models deployed in connection with Company's use for accuracy, fairness, and bias; (b) review of training-data sources, quality, and provenance; (c) assessment of explainability and transparency mechanisms; and (d) evaluation of compliance with applicable regulatory requirements, including state insurance-regulation guidance on AI use. The cost of the first annual algorithmic audit shall be borne by Vendor. The cost of any additional audits requested by Company in the same year shall be borne by Company, except that any audit triggered by a Security Incident, a material compliance concern, or a regulatory inquiry shall be at Vendor's cost regardless of the number of prior audits.
Vendor must cooperate fully with each audit, including by providing reasonable access to technical personnel, model documentation, training-data descriptions, and testing environments. Vendor may not condition cooperation on the execution of additional non-disclosure agreements beyond the confidentiality provisions of the agreement, provided that Company's auditors agree to be bound by the agreement's confidentiality terms.
Fallback Position: Vendor conducts the annual algorithmic audit using a mutually agreed independent third-party auditor (selected from a pre-approved list of at least three qualified firms). Vendor shares the full, unredacted audit report with Company within thirty (30) calendar days of the audit's completion. Company retains the right to request follow-up information or clarification, and Vendor must respond within fifteen (15) business days.
Risk Rating: Critical. Algorithmic audit rights are essential given the regulated insurance-decisioning context and the increasing regulatory scrutiny of AI use in underwriting by state regulators in Colorado, New York, and other jurisdictions where Zava operates.
3.3 Bias Testing
Required Position: Vendor must perform comprehensive bias testing on all models used in connection with Company Data on a quarterly cadence. Bias testing must evaluate model outputs for disparate impact across legally protected classes, including but not limited to race, ethnicity, gender, age, disability status, and geographic location (as a proxy for race or ethnicity, to the extent relevant under fair-lending and insurance-regulation frameworks). Bias-testing results must be delivered to Company in a structured, written report within fifteen (15) business days of the completion of each quarterly test cycle. Reports must include methodology, data sets used for testing, statistical results, identified disparities (if any), and Vendor's proposed remediation plan for any identified bias.
This provision is non-negotiable in substance. The use of AI in insurance underwriting is subject to heightened scrutiny under both existing anti-discrimination laws (including state unfair trade practices statutes) and emerging AI-specific regulations. Zava must be able to demonstrate to regulators and auditors that it has contractually required — and received — regular bias-testing results from its AI vendors.
Fallback Position: Semi-annual bias testing (rather than quarterly), with Company retaining the right to request ad hoc bias testing upon reasonable suspicion of bias or upon receipt of a regulatory inquiry related to potential discriminatory impact. Ad hoc testing triggered by a regulatory inquiry shall be conducted at Vendor's cost. Vendor must deliver ad hoc test results within twenty (20) business days of Company's request.
Risk Rating: Critical.
3.4 Model Cards
Required Position: Vendor must deliver a Model Card (as defined in Section 1.2) for each model version deployed in connection with Company's use of the Platform. Model Cards must be delivered to Company concurrently with or prior to the deployment of each model version and must be updated for each new version, including minor versions and patches that affect model behavior. Model Cards must conform to the template set forth in Appendix D of this Playbook or a substantially equivalent format agreed between the parties.
The Model Card requirement serves multiple purposes: it provides Company's underwriting, compliance, and risk-management teams with the information necessary to evaluate model suitability; it supports Company's obligations under the EU AI Act to maintain documentation for high-risk AI systems; and it creates a documentary record that can be produced to regulators upon request.
Fallback Position: Vendor provides functionally equivalent documentation covering all fields specified in the Model Card template (Appendix D), delivered within ten (10) business days of each model version release. The documentation need not be labeled a "Model Card" but must contain all required information in a structured, searchable format.
Risk Rating: High.
3.5 Explainability — NIST AI RMF
Required Position: Vendor must implement and maintain explainability capabilities consistent with the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF), specifically the "Measure" function (MEASURE 2.7 through 2.11 and related sub-categories addressing explainability and interpretability). At a minimum, Vendor must provide the capability to generate decision-level explanations for individual Outputs/Inferences upon Company's request, with a response time of no more than five (5) business days per request. Decision-level explanations must identify the principal features, data inputs, and model logic contributing to a specific Output/Inference with sufficient specificity to satisfy regulatory inquiries and consumer-explanation obligations.
Explainability is not merely a best practice — it is increasingly a regulatory requirement. Several state insurance regulators, including Colorado, have issued guidance requiring insurers to be able to explain the basis for AI-assisted underwriting decisions to consumers and regulators. Zava cannot satisfy these obligations unless its AI vendors provide adequate explainability capabilities.
Fallback Position: Vendor provides feature-importance scores or SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) value-level explanations for all underwriting-related Outputs/Inferences, together with a documented, time-bound roadmap to achieve full NIST AI RMF "Measure" function alignment within twelve (12) months of the Effective Date. The roadmap must include specific milestones, and failure to meet the roadmap milestones shall constitute a material breach of the agreement.
Risk Rating: High.
3.6 Data Lineage & Training-Data Provenance
Required Position: Vendor must provide representations and warranties regarding the lineage and provenance of all training data used in models deployed for Company, including: (a) a description of all data sources; (b) the consent, license, or other legal basis for Vendor's use of each data source; (c) the chain of custody for each data source from origin to ingestion; and (d) a representation that no training data was obtained in violation of applicable law, contractual restriction, or third-party intellectual property rights (including, without limitation, copyright, trade secret, and database rights). Vendor must promptly notify Company of any claim, allegation, or reasonable suspicion that any training data was improperly obtained.
Training-data provenance is a critical risk area in the current AI landscape. Numerous lawsuits are pending against AI companies alleging that training data was obtained in violation of copyright or other intellectual property rights. Zava must ensure that its AI vendors can demonstrate clean provenance for all training data to mitigate the risk that Company's use of the Platform could give rise to derivative liability.
Fallback Position: Vendor provides a data-provenance attestation covering first-party data (data collected or generated by Vendor) and licensed third-party data (data for which Vendor holds a valid license), together with an indemnification obligation covering any third-party claims arising from Vendor's training data. The indemnity must be included in the IP indemnification provisions of the agreement (Section 6) and must be subject to the Super-Cap (Section 5.2) or uncapped, as applicable.
Risk Rating: High.
3.7 Security Incident Response — Data Protection Overlay
Required Position: Vendor must notify Company of any Security Incident involving Company Data within twenty-four (24) hours of Vendor's discovery of the incident. A "Security Incident" includes any unauthorized access to, acquisition of, use of, disclosure of, or destruction of Company Data, whether or not the incident results in actual harm. For incidents that require notification to supervisory authorities under GDPR (which imposes a seventy-two-hour notification deadline from discovery), Vendor must notify Company sufficiently in advance to allow Company to meet its own regulatory notification obligations — and in no event later than forty-eight (48) hours after discovery.
The notification must include, at a minimum: (a) the date and time of discovery; (b) a description of the nature and scope of the incident; (c) the categories and approximate number of records affected; (d) the likely consequences of the incident; (e) the measures taken or proposed to address the incident; and (f) the identity of the Vendor personnel serving as the point of contact for incident-related communications.
Vendor must cooperate fully with Company's investigation and response efforts, including by preserving all relevant evidence, providing access to logs and systems, and participating in root-cause analysis. Vendor must not issue any public statement, press release, or notification to third parties regarding a Security Incident involving Company Data without Company's prior written consent, except as required by applicable law.
Fallback Position: Notification within seventy-two (72) hours of discovery, consistent with GDPR timelines, but Vendor must provide a preliminary incident notification within twenty-four (24) hours of discovery containing, at a minimum, the date and time of discovery, a brief description of the nature of the incident, and the point of contact. A full incident report must follow within the seventy-two-hour window.
Risk Rating: Critical.
SECTION 4 — SECURITY & AUDIT
Zava's Information Security Office has established the following minimum security and audit requirements for all AI vendor engagements. These requirements are complementary to, and do not replace, the data-protection provisions set forth in Section 3. Negotiators must ensure that both Section 3 and Section 4 requirements are fully addressed in each agreement.
4.1 SOC 2 Reports
Required Position: Vendor must maintain a current SOC 2 Type II report covering the Trust Services Criteria relevant to the Platform, including, at a minimum, the Security and Availability criteria. The report must be prepared by an independent, AICPA-accredited auditing firm and must cover an audit period of at least twelve (12) months. Vendor must deliver the most recent SOC 2 Type II report to Company within ninety (90) calendar days of the end of the audit period, and annually thereafter. SOC 2 Type I reports, which assess the design of controls at a single point in time (as opposed to the operating effectiveness of controls over a period), are insufficient for production deployments and do not satisfy this requirement.
If the SOC 2 Type II report reveals material deficiencies or exceptions, Vendor must provide a written remediation plan within thirty (30) calendar days of delivering the report, and Company may exercise enhanced audit rights under Section 4.3 until the deficiencies are remediated and verified.
Fallback Position: If Vendor is in the process of transitioning from a SOC 2 Type I report to a SOC 2 Type II report (for example, if Vendor has recently engaged an auditing firm and the Type II audit period has not yet concluded), Vendor must deliver a SOC 2 Type II report within one hundred eighty (180) days of the Effective Date. During the interim period, Company may exercise enhanced audit rights under Section 4.3, including the right to conduct an on-site or remote security assessment of Vendor's controls. Vendor must provide its most recent SOC 2 Type I report and any available bridge letters or interim attestations during this period.
Risk Rating: Critical. A SOC 2 Type I report alone is unacceptable for production deployments involving Company Data. If Vendor cannot commit to delivering a SOC 2 Type II report within the timeframes specified above, escalate to Emil Vanggaard and the Information Security Office for a risk assessment.
4.2 Penetration Testing
Required Position: Company has the right to conduct, or to commission a qualified third party to conduct, an annual penetration test of the Platform and all related infrastructure used to process, store, or transmit Company Data, upon thirty (30) calendar days' prior written notice to Vendor. The scope of the penetration test shall be mutually agreed in advance, but Vendor may not unreasonably restrict the scope to exclude critical system components. Vendor must remediate all critical and high-severity findings within thirty (30) calendar days of delivery of the penetration-test report, and all medium-severity findings within sixty (60) calendar days. Vendor must provide Company with evidence of remediation upon completion. Low-severity findings must be addressed within ninety (90) calendar days or included in Vendor's standard remediation cycle, whichever is sooner.
Fallback Position: Vendor conducts an annual penetration test using a mutually agreed, independent third-party firm selected from a pre-approved list. Vendor shares the full, unredacted penetration-test report with Company within thirty (30) calendar days of the test's completion. Company retains the right to conduct its own penetration test if: (a) Vendor's report reveals critical or high-severity findings that, in Company's reasonable judgment, have not been adequately remediated; (b) a Security Incident has occurred; or (c) Company's Information Security Office identifies a reasonable basis for additional testing based on threat-intelligence information.
Risk Rating: High.
4.3 On-Site / Remote Audit Rights
Required Position: Company has the right to conduct on-site or remote audits of Vendor's facilities, systems, processes, and records relevant to the Platform and Company Data, at least once per year upon fifteen (15) business days' prior written notice to Vendor. The scope of the audit may include, without limitation, review of security controls, access-management practices, change-management procedures, backup and disaster-recovery capabilities, and compliance with the agreement's data-protection and privacy provisions. Company may also conduct ad hoc audits upon the occurrence of a Security Incident, a material compliance concern, or a regulatory inquiry, with reasonable notice under the circumstances (which may be less than fifteen business days for urgent matters).
Company may designate its own personnel or qualified third-party auditors to conduct the audit. Vendor must provide reasonable cooperation, including making available relevant documentation, systems, and personnel. Vendor may not charge Company for the costs of Vendor's cooperation with audits.
Fallback Position: Audits are limited to once per calendar year unless a Security Incident or regulatory inquiry occurs, in which case Company may conduct additional audits as reasonably necessary. Vendor may designate a reasonable chaperone to accompany Company's auditors during on-site visits and may require Company's third-party auditors to execute non-disclosure agreements consistent with the agreement's confidentiality provisions. However, Vendor may not redact or withhold any information that is material to Company's audit objectives, and any confidentiality restrictions on audit findings may not prevent Company from sharing audit results with its regulators, legal counsel, or auditors.
Risk Rating: High.
SECTION 5 — LIABILITY
Liability provisions are among the most heavily negotiated terms in AI vendor agreements. Vendors routinely propose liability caps that are grossly inadequate relative to the risks inherent in high-value, high-risk AI deployments in regulated industries. The positions set forth in this Section establish Zava's minimum acceptable liability framework and provide negotiators with the benchmarks necessary to evaluate and counter vendor proposals.
5.1 General Liability Cap
Required Position: The aggregate liability cap for each party under the agreement shall be no less than two times (2×) the ACV of the agreement. For an engagement with an ACV of $2,950,000, the general liability cap is $5,900,000. This cap applies to all claims arising under or in connection with the agreement, except for those categories of liability that are subject to the Super-Cap (Section 5.2) or that are uncapped (Section 5.3).
The 2× ACV standard reflects the magnitude of potential losses in the event of a significant vendor failure — including but not limited to model errors that result in systematic underwriting losses, data breaches that trigger regulatory fines and litigation costs, and IP infringement claims that impair Company's ability to use the Platform. A cap set at a fraction of annual fees (as is typical in vendor standard forms) would leave Company bearing the vast majority of loss exposure, which is commercially unreasonable given the vendor's role as the provider and operator of the AI platform.
Fallback Position: Eighteen (18) months' fees paid or payable under the agreement as an absolute floor. However, the 2× ACV standard is strongly preferred and should be the negotiating target in all cases. The 18-month fallback should be used only when the vendor has demonstrated a credible commercial reason for resisting the 2× standard and when the deal team has exhausted good-faith negotiation efforts. Any cap below 18 months' fees requires Emil Vanggaard's approval.
Risk Rating: Critical. Any proposed liability cap below 2× ACV requires approval from Emil Vanggaard. Any proposed cap below 18 months' fees is presumptively unacceptable and must be escalated with a detailed risk justification.
5.2 Super-Cap (Enhanced Liability Categories)
Required Position: The following categories of liability shall be subject to an enhanced cap (the "Super-Cap") equal to three times (3×) the ACV of the agreement. For an engagement with an ACV of $2,950,000, the Super-Cap is $8,850,000. The Super-Cap applies separately and in addition to the general liability cap — meaning that a party's aggregate liability under the Super-Cap categories is subject to the 3× ACV limit, and its aggregate liability under all other categories is subject to the general 2× ACV limit:
•  Intellectual property infringement: Claims, damages, and costs arising from a breach of IP representations and warranties or from Vendor's infringement of third-party intellectual property rights (to the extent not uncapped under Section 5.3).
•  Data breach: Claims, damages, and costs arising from unauthorized access to, acquisition of, use of, disclosure of, or destruction of Company Data, including regulatory fines, notification costs, credit-monitoring costs, and litigation expenses.
•  Breach of confidentiality obligations: Claims, damages, and costs arising from Vendor's unauthorized disclosure or use of Company's confidential information.
Fallback Position: Super-Cap at two and one-half times (2.5×) ACV, but only if the general liability cap is set at the Required Position of 2× ACV. Under no circumstances should the Super-Cap be set lower than the general cap itself, as this would render the Super-Cap meaningless. For the example engagement (ACV of $2,950,000), the fallback Super-Cap would be $7,375,000.
Risk Rating: Critical.
5.3 Uncapped Liability Categories
Required Position: The following categories of liability shall be carved out from all liability caps — both the general cap and the Super-Cap — and shall be uncapped (i.e., each party's liability under these categories shall not be subject to any contractual limitation of liability):
•  Fraud or intentional misrepresentation by either party.
•  Willful misconduct or gross negligence by either party.
•  Vendor's third-party IP indemnification obligations under Section 6 of this Playbook (and the corresponding provision of the agreement).
These categories are carved out because they involve culpable conduct (fraud, willful misconduct) or third-party exposure (IP indemnification) for which a contractual cap would either be unenforceable as a matter of public policy or would leave Company bearing losses that are properly allocated to the party at fault.
Fallback Position: None. [HARD STOP] No deviation is permitted from this position. Vendors may resist uncapped carve-outs, but the categories specified above are standard uncapped categories in enterprise technology agreements and are widely accepted in the market. If a vendor refuses to accept uncapped liability for fraud, willful misconduct, and IP indemnification, the deal team should seriously question the vendor's good faith and escalate to Emil Vanggaard.
Risk Rating: Critical.
5.4 Vendor Liability Cap Benchmarks
Vendor proposals frequently offer liability caps of six (6) or twelve (12) months' fees paid or payable under the agreement. These proposals are inadequate for high-value, high-risk AI deployments in regulated industries and should be rejected. The following illustration demonstrates the inadequacy of a 6-month cap:
For an engagement with an Annual Platform Fee of $2,710,000 and an annual implementation/professional-services fee of $240,000 (total ACV of $2,950,000), a 6-month cap would limit Vendor's aggregate liability to approximately $1,355,000 (half of the Annual Platform Fee) or $1,475,000 (half of ACV, depending on the cap calculation methodology). This amount would be insufficient to cover even the direct costs of a significant data breach (notification, credit monitoring, forensic investigation, and regulatory fines), let alone consequential damages from model errors that result in systematic underwriting losses. By contrast, the Required Position (2× ACV) would provide a general cap of $5,900,000, which, while not fully compensatory in a worst-case scenario, provides a more meaningful remedy.
Negotiators should use these benchmarks to frame the discussion with vendors and to demonstrate the commercial reasonableness of Zava's Required Position. If a vendor insists on a cap below 18 months' fees, the deal team should explore whether enhanced insurance requirements (Section 7) or a vendor parent-company guarantee can mitigate the gap.
SECTION 6 — INDEMNIFICATION
Robust indemnification provisions are essential to protect Zava against third-party claims arising from the vendor's products, services, and conduct. Given the novel and evolving legal landscape surrounding AI-generated outputs, training-data provenance, and algorithmic bias, the indemnification framework must address both traditional IP infringement risks and AI-specific risks.
6.1 Intellectual Property Indemnification
Required Position: Vendor must indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Company and its officers, directors, employees, and agents ("Company Indemnified Parties") against all third-party claims, actions, suits, proceedings, losses, damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees and costs of litigation) alleging that Company's use of the Platform, as authorized under the agreement, infringes or misappropriates any:
•  Patent (whether utility or design)
•  Copyright (including rights in software, databases, and creative works)
•  Trade secret
•  Trademark or service mark
•  Other intellectual property right of any third party
The indemnity must cover all costs of defense (including the obligation to advance defense costs), all settlements entered into with Company's prior written consent, and all final judgments and damages awarded by a court of competent jurisdiction. Vendor's indemnification obligation must be primary and not contingent on Company's exhaustion of any other remedy or insurance coverage.
In addition to the indemnification obligation, Vendor must include a standard "cure" provision: if the Platform is found to infringe or if Vendor reasonably believes it may infringe, Vendor must, at its expense, either (a) procure the right for Company to continue using the Platform, (b) modify the Platform to render it non-infringing without materially diminishing functionality, or (c) replace the Platform with a non-infringing alternative of substantially equivalent functionality. If none of these options is commercially feasible, Company may terminate the agreement and Vendor must refund all prepaid, unearned fees and provide transition assistance under Section 11.
Fallback Position: Vendor may limit the geographic scope of the indemnity to claims arising in the United States, provided that the indemnity must be extended to cover claims arising in the European Union if Company processes EU data through the Platform. This geographic limitation is acceptable only because Zava's operations are currently concentrated in the United States and the EU; if Zava expands into other jurisdictions, the indemnity scope must be revisited.
Risk Rating: Critical.
6.2 AI Output Indemnity
Required Position: In addition to the standard IP indemnification under Section 6.1, Vendor must indemnify Company Indemnified Parties against third-party claims arising from the content or nature of AI-generated Outputs/Inferences produced by the Platform, including but not limited to:
•  Infringement claims: Claims alleging that an Output/Inference infringes a third party's copyright, right of publicity, or other intellectual property right (for example, a claim that an AI-generated report or analysis incorporates copyrighted material from the Vendor's training data).
•  Defamation claims: Claims alleging that an Output/Inference contains defamatory statements about a third party (for example, a claim that an AI-generated risk assessment contains false and injurious statements about an individual or entity).
This indemnity applies to the extent the Output/Inference was generated by the Platform without material modification by Company. If Company materially modifies an Output/Inference (for example, by editing, supplementing, or incorporating it into a larger work), the indemnity applies only to the unmodified portions attributable to the Platform.
The AI Output Indemnity addresses a risk that is unique to AI vendor agreements and is not covered by traditional IP indemnification provisions. Because AI models may generate outputs that inadvertently reproduce copyrighted material, reflect training-data biases, or contain inaccurate statements, the risk of third-party claims arising from AI-generated content is real and growing. Company should not bear this risk, because Company has no visibility into or control over the training data, model architecture, or inference processes that produce Outputs.
Fallback Position: AI Output Indemnity limited to Outputs/Inferences generated using Vendor's base models (i.e., models that have not been fine-tuned using Company Data), with Company accepting risk for Outputs generated by fine-tuned models. This fallback reflects the shared responsibility for fine-tuned models: Vendor contributes the base model and training methodology, while Company contributes the fine-tuning data. However, even under this fallback, Vendor's indemnity should cover claims attributable to the base model's pre-existing training data (as opposed to Company's fine-tuning data).
Risk Rating: High.
6.3 Indemnification Procedures
The agreement must include standard indemnification procedures that govern the process for tendering, defending, and resolving indemnification claims. At a minimum, the procedures must address the following:
•  Prompt Notice: The indemnified party must provide prompt written notice to the indemnifying party of any claim for which indemnification is sought. However, failure to provide prompt notice shall not relieve the indemnifying party of its indemnification obligations except to the extent the indemnifying party is materially prejudiced by the delay.
•  Control of Defense: The indemnifying party has the right to assume and control the defense of the claim, including the selection of counsel, provided that the indemnifying party's counsel must be reasonably acceptable to the indemnified party. The indemnified party has the right to participate in the defense at its own expense with counsel of its own choosing.
•  Cooperation: The indemnified party must provide reasonable cooperation to the indemnifying party in the defense of the claim, including by providing access to relevant documents, information, and personnel.
•  Settlement: The indemnifying party may not settle any claim without the indemnified party's prior written consent, which shall not be unreasonably withheld, conditioned, or delayed. In no event may the indemnifying party agree to a settlement that (a) imposes any obligation, restriction, or liability on the indemnified party, (b) admits fault or liability on behalf of the indemnified party, or (c) includes non-monetary relief affecting the indemnified party, without the indemnified party's express written consent.

SECTION 8 — FEES & ESCALATION
Fee provisions in multi-year AI vendor agreements have a significant impact on total cost of ownership. Vendors frequently propose aggressive annual fee escalators and volume-pricing structures that, if accepted without scrutiny, can substantially inflate the TCV of the engagement over the initial term. The positions set forth in this Section are designed to ensure predictable, controlled fee growth and to protect Company against hidden cost increases.
8.1 Fee Escalator Cap
Required Position: Annual fee escalators shall not exceed the Consumer Price Index (CPI), U.S. City Average, All Items, as published by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, plus one percentage point (CPI + 1%), with a hard cap of three percent (3%) in any contract year, regardless of the CPI level. The escalator applies to all recurring fees under the agreement, including platform fees, subscription fees, and support fees. The escalator does not apply to one-time fees (such as implementation fees) or to fees for professional services priced on a time-and-materials basis.
The CPI + 1% / 3% hard-cap structure provides a reasonable balance between the vendor's interest in protecting against cost inflation and the Company's interest in predictable, manageable fee growth. The 3% hard cap is essential to protect Company in inflationary environments where CPI may spike (as occurred in 2022–2023).
For the first contract year, no escalator applies; the initial-year fees are fixed as set forth in the order form.
Fallback Position: CPI plus one and one-half percentage points (CPI + 1.5%), with a hard cap of four percent (4%) in any contract year. However, this fallback may be accepted only if the vendor agrees to reduce the initial-year platform fee by at least five percent (5%) from the originally proposed amount. This concession offsets the higher escalator cap by reducing the base from which the escalator is calculated.
