SECTION 9 — MODEL GOVERNANCE & CHANGE CONTROL
Model governance and change control are uniquely important in AI vendor agreements. Unlike traditional software, where updates and patches are generally incremental and predictable, AI model changes can fundamentally alter the behavior, accuracy, and fairness of the system. In a regulated insurance-decisioning context, an unauthorized or poorly managed model change could result in systematic underwriting errors, discriminatory outcomes, or regulatory violations — any of which could have severe consequences for Zava.
9.1 Material Model Changes — Notice and Approval
Required Position: Vendor must provide Company with at least sixty (60) calendar days' advance written notice before implementing any Material Model Change in connection with Company's use of the Platform. Company must provide prior written approval before any Material Model Change is deployed in production for Company's use. Vendor may not deploy a Material Model Change in Company's production environment without Company's express written approval, and Company may withhold approval for any reason, including without limitation concerns about model accuracy, fairness, explainability, regulatory compliance, or operational impact.
As defined in Section 1.2, a "Material Model Change" means any modification to a model that results in greater than two percent (2%) variance in output distribution (as measured against a representative validation data set agreed between the parties), or any change to the sources of training data used in models deployed for Company. The 2% threshold is designed to capture changes that have a meaningful impact on model behavior while excluding routine maintenance updates and bug fixes.
The 60-day notice period and approval right are essential to allow Company's underwriting, compliance, and AI strategy teams to evaluate the proposed change, conduct independent testing, and assess regulatory implications before the change affects live underwriting pipelines. Luc Lacombe's underwriting team, in particular, requires sufficient lead time to adjust underwriting workflows, retrain staff, and update downstream systems.
Fallback Position: Forty-five (45) calendar days' advance written notice, with Company's right to reject the change and revert to the prior model version within thirty (30) calendar days of deployment if the change materially and adversely affects Company's operations (including disruption to live underwriting pipelines, degradation of model accuracy or fairness, or increased regulatory risk). If Company exercises its revert right, Vendor must restore the prior model version within five (5) business days and must bear all costs associated with the reversion, including any costs of re-processing decisions made during the period the new model version was deployed.
Risk Rating: Critical. Vendor standard forms frequently include fifteen (15)-day notice periods without any approval rights, which are wholly inadequate for regulated insurance decisioning. Any notice period shorter than 45 days or any agreement that does not include an approval right (or, at minimum, a revert right) must be escalated to Emil Vanggaard and Luc Lacombe.
9.2 Deprecated Models — Continued Availability
Required Position: When Vendor deprecates a model version that is currently deployed in connection with Company's use of the Platform, Vendor must continue to make the deprecated model version available to Company — fully functional, supported, and at the same service levels as the current production model — for a period of not less than twelve (12) months following written notice of deprecation, at no additional cost to Company. During this period, Vendor must provide Company with migration support, including documentation, testing environments, and technical assistance, to facilitate Company's transition to the successor model version.
This provision protects Company against forced migrations that disrupt operations. AI model migrations are complex and require extensive testing, validation, and regulatory review. A vendor-imposed deprecation with a short sunset period could force Company to adopt a new model version before Company has had the opportunity to evaluate its accuracy, fairness, and regulatory compliance.
Fallback Position: Nine (9) months' continued availability of the deprecated model version following written notice of deprecation, with Vendor providing migration support at no additional charge. If the 9-month period is insufficient for Company to complete its migration (for example, due to regulatory-review timelines), Company may request an extension of up to three (3) additional months, which Vendor shall not unreasonably refuse.
Risk Rating: High.
9.3 Model Versioning and Documentation
Vendor must maintain and provide a complete version history for all models deployed in connection with Company's use of the Platform. The version history must include, for each version:
•  Version number and release date
•  A description of changes from the prior version
•  The training data used (including any changes to training-data sources)
•  Performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC) measured against the agreed validation data set
•  A Model Card (as required by Section 3.4) for each version
•  Updated bias-testing results (as required by Section 3.3) for each version that constitutes a Material Model Change
Vendor must maintain version-history records for the life of the agreement and for a period of not less than seven (7) years following termination, consistent with insurance-industry record-retention requirements. Vendor must make version-history records available to Company upon request within ten (10) business days.
SECTION 10 — SUBCONTRACTING
AI vendor supply chains are often opaque, involving multiple layers of subcontractors for cloud infrastructure, data processing, model training, and support services. Each subcontractor in the chain represents a potential point of failure and a potential source of data-protection, security, and IP risk. The provisions in this Section ensure that Company maintains visibility and control over the subcontractor ecosystem and that Vendor remains fully accountable for its subcontractors' performance.
10.1 Consent Requirements
Required Position: Vendor may not subcontract any of the following activities without Company's prior written consent, which Company may grant or withhold in its sole discretion:
•  Model training or fine-tuning: Any activity in which a subcontractor trains, retrains, fine-tunes, or otherwise modifies AI/ML models using Company Data or in connection with Company's use of the Platform.
•  Data processing or storage of Company Data: Any activity in which a subcontractor processes, stores, accesses, or transmits Company Data, including policyholder data, underwriting data, and any data that constitutes personal information under applicable privacy laws.
•  Hosting or infrastructure services for the Platform: Any activity in which a subcontractor provides cloud computing, hosting, storage, or other infrastructure services used to operate the Platform or store Company Data.
Company's consent process for subcontractor requests will include review by the Technology Transactions team (for contractual compliance), the Information Security Office (for security posture), and the relevant business-unit stakeholder (for operational impact). The consent process should be completed within fifteen (15) business days of receipt of a complete subcontractor information package from Vendor.
Fallback Position: Pre-approved subcontractors that are listed in an exhibit to the agreement at the time of execution may perform hosting and infrastructure services without case-by-case consent, provided that the exhibit includes sufficient detail about each subcontractor's identity, jurisdiction, and scope of services. However, model training and fine-tuning activities, as well as data processing involving Company Data, require case-by-case consent regardless of whether the subcontractor is pre-approved. Any addition of a new subcontractor to the pre-approved list requires Company's prior written consent.
Risk Rating: Critical for model training and data processing; High for hosting and infrastructure.
10.2 Subcontractor Liability Flow-Down
Required Position: Vendor shall be fully liable for all acts, omissions, errors, negligence, and breaches of its subcontractors (including subcontractors at all tiers) as if such acts, omissions, errors, negligence, and breaches were performed by Vendor itself. Vendor must ensure that all subcontracts include obligations that are at least as protective of Company as the corresponding terms of the agreement, including without limitation data-protection, security, confidentiality, and IP ownership provisions. The existence of a subcontract does not relieve Vendor of any obligation under the agreement.
Fallback Position: None. [HARD STOP] No deviation is permitted from this position. Full subcontractor liability flow-down is a fundamental risk-allocation principle that ensures Company has a single point of accountability (Vendor) for all services performed under the agreement, regardless of how Vendor structures its supply chain.
Risk Rating: Critical.
10.3 Subcontractor List Maintenance
Required Position: Vendor must maintain a current, accurate list of all subcontractors performing services under the agreement (the "Subcontractor List"). The Subcontractor List must be attached to the agreement as a formal exhibit (not buried in an Acceptable Use Policy, privacy policy, or other ancillary document that Vendor may update unilaterally). The Subcontractor List must include the information specified in the Subcontractor List Template (Appendix C), including legal name, jurisdiction of organization, description of services performed, level of access to Company Data, and the date of Company's consent. Vendor must update the Subcontractor List within five (5) business days of any addition, removal, or change of subcontractor.
Fallback Position: Updates within ten (10) business days of any change, with Company retaining the right to object to any new subcontractor within fifteen (15) business days of notification. If Company objects, Vendor must not use the objected-to subcontractor until the parties have resolved the objection through good-faith discussion. If the parties cannot resolve the objection within thirty (30) calendar days, Company may terminate the agreement upon sixty (60) days' notice without penalty.
Risk Rating: Medium.
SECTION 11 — TERMINATION & TRANSITION
The provisions in this Section are governed by the anti-lock-in principles set forth in Section 11.5. Every termination and transition provision must be evaluated through the lens of vendor portability: the goal is to ensure that Company can transition away from any single AI vendor without operational disruption, data loss, or unreasonable cost. AI platform migrations are inherently complex, and the contractual framework must account for the time, resources, and technical challenges involved.
11.1 Transition Period
Required Position: Upon expiration or termination of the agreement (for any reason, including termination for convenience, termination for cause, and expiration of the initial term without renewal), the agreement must provide a transition period of not less than one hundred eighty (180) calendar days during which Vendor continues to perform all material services under the agreement — at the then-current fee levels and service levels — to enable Company to migrate to a successor solution without disruption to live operations. The transition period is particularly critical for underwriting pipelines, where any gap in AI-assisted decisioning capability could result in processing delays, increased manual workload, and potential regulatory issues.
During the transition period, Vendor must cooperate fully with Company and any successor vendor designated by Company, including by providing access to APIs, documentation, data exports, and technical personnel. Vendor may not use the transition period as leverage to negotiate renewal or other commercial concessions.
Fallback Position: One hundred twenty (120) calendar days, but only if Vendor agrees to the enhanced transition-services obligation set forth in Section 11.3 (i.e., up to 12 months of transition-services support at controlled rates). The shorter transition period is acceptable only if Company has confidence that the 120-day window, combined with extended transition services, provides sufficient time to complete the migration.
Risk Rating: Critical. A ninety (90)-day wind-down period is inadequate for complex AI platform migrations and must be rejected. Vendor proposals for "commercially reasonable wind-down assistance" without a specified minimum period are also unacceptable — the transition period must be a defined contractual commitment with specific obligations.
11.2 Data Return
Required Position: Vendor must return all Company Data — including Fine-Tuned Model Weights, Outputs/Inferences, training-data derivatives, embeddings, vectors, metadata, configuration data, and all other data belonging to Company — in Apache Parquet format or CSV format (as specified by Company) within thirty (30) calendar days of the date of termination notice. Vendor's proprietary data formats are not acceptable for data return, as they create vendor lock-in and may impede Company's ability to use the data with a successor platform or for internal analysis.
Data return must be accompanied by a complete data dictionary describing the structure, schema, and content of all returned data files. Vendor must provide reasonable technical support to assist Company in validating the completeness and integrity of the returned data.
Upon completion of data return and Company's written confirmation of receipt and validation, Vendor must certify in writing — signed by an authorized officer of Vendor — the destruction of all copies of Company Data (including all backups, archives, logs, and derivative copies) within fifteen (15) business days. The destruction certification must specify the method of destruction used and confirm that no copies of Company Data remain in Vendor's possession, custody, or control (or in the possession of any subcontractor). Vendor must retain the destruction certification for a period of seven (7) years.
Fallback Position: Data return in JSON format or another industry-standard, open, non-proprietary format if Apache Parquet or CSV is technically infeasible for certain data types (for example, complex nested data structures or binary model-weight files). The alternative format must be agreed in advance by Company's technical team, and Company must provide prior written agreement to the use of the alternative format. Under no circumstances may Vendor return Company Data exclusively in a proprietary format.
Risk Rating: Critical. Proprietary-format-only data return creates vendor lock-in and is a [HARD STOP]. If a vendor insists on returning data exclusively in a proprietary format, the deal team must escalate to Emil Vanggaard and consider whether the engagement should proceed.
11.3 Transition Services
Required Position: Vendor must provide transition-assistance services for a period of up to twelve (12) months following the effective date of termination (the "Transition Services Period"), at rates not exceeding one hundred ten percent (110%) of the then-current fees under the agreement. The 10% premium is intended to compensate Vendor for the incremental cost of supporting a transitioning customer; rates exceeding 110% create a financial disincentive for Company to exercise its transition rights and are unacceptable.
Transition services must include, at a minimum:
•  Knowledge transfer sessions with Company's technical team and any successor vendor
•  Continued API access for data extraction and integration testing
•  Access to documentation, including all Model Cards, version histories, and technical specifications
•  Reasonable technical support for migration to a successor platform, including assistance with data mapping, format conversion, and validation
•  Cooperation with Company's designated successor vendor, including participation in joint planning meetings and provision of technical specifications necessary for the successor vendor to replicate or replace the Platform's functionality
Fallback Position: A six (6)-month Transition Services Period at one hundred twenty percent (120%) of then-current fees, with Company's right to extend for an additional six (6) months at one hundred thirty percent (130%) of then-current fees. This fallback is acceptable only if the combined maximum Transition Services Period (12 months) provides the same total coverage as the Required Position. The escalating rate structure is a concession to Vendor's interest in limiting the duration of post-termination obligations, offset by Company's extension right.
Risk Rating: High.
11.4 Source-Code Escrow
Required Position: Vendor must enter into a source-code escrow agreement with Iron Mountain Intellectual Property Management, Inc. (or its successor) as the escrow agent, with Company as a named beneficiary of the escrow. Vendor must deposit into escrow all source code, object code, build scripts, documentation, and related materials necessary to compile, build, deploy, and operate the Platform (collectively, the "Escrow Materials"). Escrow Materials must be updated at least annually and upon each major version release.
The escrow agreement must include the following release triggers, upon the occurrence of any of which the escrow agent shall release the Escrow Materials to Company:
•  Insolvency: Vendor becomes insolvent, files a petition in bankruptcy, has an involuntary petition in bankruptcy filed against it that is not dismissed within sixty (60) days, makes an assignment for the benefit of creditors, or is the subject of receivership, liquidation, or similar proceedings.
•  Material Breach: Vendor commits a material breach of the agreement that remains uncured for sixty (60) days after Company's written notice of breach.
•  Cessation of Business: Vendor ceases business operations or discontinues the Platform (whether by notice, de facto abandonment, or failure to provide updates or support for a period of twelve (12) consecutive months).
Upon release of the Escrow Materials, Company receives a non-exclusive, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, modify, compile, and deploy the Escrow Materials solely for Company's internal business purposes, including the operation and maintenance of the Platform.
Fallback Position: Vendor may propose an alternative nationally recognized escrow agent (such as EscrowTech International, Inc. or NCC Group), subject to Company's approval (which shall not be unreasonably withheld). Iron Mountain Intellectual Property Management, Inc. is strongly preferred due to its industry-leading position and Zava's existing escrow-agent relationship. The escrow release triggers specified above are non-negotiable and must be included regardless of the escrow agent selected.
Risk Rating: Critical. Source-code escrow is a key portability protection, and its absence from an AI vendor agreement is unacceptable. If a vendor refuses to agree to escrow, the deal team must escalate to Emil Vanggaard for a proceed/no-proceed determination.
11.5 Anti-Lock-In Principles
The overarching objective of this Section — and a guiding principle of this entire Playbook — is to ensure that Zava is never operationally or contractually locked in to any single AI vendor. The AI vendor market is dynamic and rapidly evolving, and Zava's competitive position depends on its ability to select, change, and combine AI vendor solutions based on performance, cost, and strategic alignment. Vendor lock-in impairs this flexibility and creates unacceptable concentration risk.
All termination and transition provisions must be evaluated through this anti-lock-in lens. Negotiators should scrutinize every clause in the agreement for potential lock-in effects, including but not limited to:
•  Proprietary data formats that prevent or impede data portability
•  Exclusive-use restrictions that prevent Company from engaging competing AI vendors
•  Early-termination penalties that create a financial disincentive for Company to exit the relationship
•  Restrictive post-termination covenants that limit Company's ability to use data, models, or outputs after termination
•  Auto-renewal provisions with late-notice deadlines that effectively extend the term without Company's affirmative consent
•  Switching penalties or migration fees imposed by Vendor in connection with Company's transition to a successor platform
Any clause that exhibits one or more of these lock-in characteristics should be flagged for negotiation or deletion. If Vendor refuses to address a material lock-in concern, the deal team should escalate to Emil Vanggaard for guidance.
SECTION 12 — GOVERNING LAW & DISPUTE RESOLUTION
Governing law and dispute resolution provisions determine the legal framework and forum in which any disputes under the agreement will be resolved. These provisions are important not only for practical reasons (familiarity of counsel, proximity to witnesses, judicial expertise) but also for substantive reasons (the choice of governing law can affect the interpretation and enforceability of key contractual provisions, including limitation-of-liability clauses, indemnification obligations, and intellectual property rights).
12.1 Governing Law
Required Position: The agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the State of Delaware, without regard to its conflict-of-laws principles. Delaware law is preferred because Zava is incorporated in Delaware, Delaware courts have extensive experience adjudicating complex commercial and technology disputes, and Delaware's body of corporate and commercial law is well-developed and predictable.
Fallback Position: New York law is an acceptable alternative. Zava's principal place of business is in Stamford, Connecticut, and New York law is the most commonly chosen governing law for complex commercial agreements in the tri-state area. New York's courts have deep experience with technology and financial-services disputes, and New York law provides robust protections for contractual rights. However, negotiators should prefer Delaware law where possible.
Texas law, California law, or any other vendor-home-state law is not acceptable unless specifically approved by Emil Vanggaard after a conflict-of-laws analysis by the Technology Transactions team. Zava has no significant nexus to most vendor-home states, and the choice of an unfamiliar governing law introduces unnecessary risk and cost.
Risk Rating: High.
12.2 Dispute Resolution — Forum
Required Position: All disputes arising out of or relating to the agreement shall be resolved by litigation in the Delaware Court of Chancery (or, if the Court of Chancery declines jurisdiction, the Superior Court of the State of Delaware) or the United States District Court for the District of Delaware. Each party shall irrevocably consent to the exclusive jurisdiction and venue of these courts and waive any objection based on forum non conveniens or any similar doctrine.
The Delaware Court of Chancery is the preferred forum for several reasons: (a) it is a specialized court with expertise in commercial, corporate, and technology disputes; (b) it offers expedited proceedings and experienced chancellors; (c) it sits without a jury, which reduces the unpredictability of outcomes; and (d) Zava's incorporation in Delaware provides a natural jurisdictional nexus.
Fallback Position: The United States District Court for the Southern District of New York is an acceptable alternative forum. The Southern District has extensive experience with complex commercial litigation and is conveniently located for Zava's Stamford-based legal and executive team. If New York is agreed as the forum, the governing law should also be changed to New York law for consistency (see Section 12.1).
Risk Rating: High.
12.3 No Mandatory Arbitration
Required Position: The agreement shall not include any mandatory binding arbitration clause, whether administered by JAMS, the American Arbitration Association (AAA), the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), or any other arbitration provider. Company reserves the right to seek all remedies available at law and in equity, including injunctive and declaratory relief, in a court of competent jurisdiction. Any arbitration clause in Vendor's standard form must be deleted in its entirety.
Mandatory arbitration is unacceptable for several reasons: (a) arbitration limits the scope of discovery, which can impede Company's ability to develop the factual record necessary to prove complex technology and data-breach claims; (b) arbitration awards are subject to extremely limited judicial review, which reduces the predictability and quality of outcomes; (c) arbitration proceedings and awards are typically confidential, which may conflict with Company's regulatory-disclosure obligations; and (d) the cost of arbitration (including arbitrator fees) can be significant, particularly in multi-party or multi-claim disputes.
Fallback Position: None. [HARD STOP] No deviation is permitted from this position. JAMS arbitration clauses, AAA arbitration clauses, and all other mandatory arbitration provisions must be deleted. If a vendor categorically refuses to delete a mandatory arbitration clause, the deal team must escalate to Emil Vanggaard for a proceed/no-proceed determination.
Risk Rating: Critical.
12.4 No Class-Action Waiver
Required Position: The agreement shall not include any class-action waiver, collective-action waiver, or any waiver of Company's right to participate in, bring, or be a member of representative actions, class actions, or consolidated proceedings. Such waivers are frequently included in vendor standard forms (particularly those drafted by consumer-facing technology companies) and must be deleted.
Fallback Position: None. [HARD STOP] No deviation is permitted. Class-action waivers are inappropriate in commercial agreements between sophisticated enterprise parties and may impair Company's ability to participate in or benefit from class actions brought against vendors for widespread harms (such as data breaches affecting multiple customers).
Risk Rating: Critical.
12.5 Jury-Trial Waiver
A mutual jury-trial waiver — in which both parties waive the right to a trial by jury for any dispute arising under the agreement — is permissible and acceptable. This is consistent with Zava's preferred forum (Delaware Court of Chancery, which is an equitable court that does not empanel juries) and with federal-court practice (where bench trials are common in complex commercial cases). A mutual waiver eliminates jury-trial unpredictability for both parties and is widely accepted in enterprise technology agreements.
However, a unilateral jury-trial waiver — in which only Company waives the right to a jury trial while Vendor retains that right — is not acceptable and must be rejected. Any jury-trial waiver must be mutual and symmetrical.
Risk Rating: Low (mutual waiver is acceptable and consistent with Zava's preferred forum strategy).

SECTION 14 — HARD STOPS — NON-NEGOTIABLE POSITIONS
The following positions are designated as hard stops throughout this Playbook. A hard stop is a contractual position that may not be conceded under any circumstance, regardless of ACV band, commercial pressure, vendor-relationship considerations, or executive direction. Hard stops represent Zava's absolute minimum requirements — the floor below which the Company will not go.
If a vendor refuses to accept one or more hard-stop positions after good-faith negotiation, the deal team must escalate to the General Counsel for a proceed/no-proceed determination. The General Counsel has sole authority to determine whether a deal should proceed notwithstanding a vendor's refusal to accept a hard-stop position, and any such determination must be documented in writing with a detailed risk analysis.
The hard-stop positions are as follows:
1.  Company Sole Ownership of Outputs/Inferences (Section 2.2). All Outputs/Inferences generated by the Platform in response to Company Data inputs are the sole and exclusive property of Company. Vendor receives no rights in Outputs/Inferences except as strictly necessary to perform the services during the term. No fallback position exists for this issue.
2.  Uncapped Liability for Fraud, Willful Misconduct, and Third-Party IP Indemnification (Section 5.3). Liability for fraud or intentional misrepresentation, willful misconduct or gross negligence, and Vendor's third-party IP indemnification obligations must be carved out from all liability caps and remain uncapped. No fallback position exists for this issue.
3.  Full Subcontractor Liability Flow-Down (Section 10.2). Vendor must be fully liable for all acts, omissions, and breaches of its subcontractors as if performed by Vendor itself. All subcontracts must include obligations at least as protective of Company as the terms of the agreement. No fallback position exists for this issue.
4.  No Mandatory Binding Arbitration (Section 12.3). The agreement must not include any mandatory binding arbitration clause, whether administered by JAMS, AAA, ICC, or any other arbitration provider. All arbitration clauses must be deleted. No fallback position exists for this issue.
5.  No Class-Action Waiver (Section 12.4). The agreement must not include any class-action waiver, collective-action waiver, or waiver of Company's right to participate in or bring representative actions. No fallback position exists for this issue.
6.  Data Return in Open, Non-Proprietary Formats (Section 11.2). Upon termination, Vendor must return all Company Data in Apache Parquet, CSV, or another industry-standard open format (with Company's prior written agreement). Vendor's proprietary formats are not acceptable as the sole or primary format for data return. No deviation is permitted that would result in Company receiving its data exclusively in a proprietary format.
These six hard-stop positions are non-negotiable and represent the absolute minimum protections that Zava requires in every AI vendor agreement. APPENDIX A — SERVICE LEVEL REQUIREMENTS TEMPLATE
Purpose. This Appendix sets forth the standard Service Level Agreement (SLA) framework to be incorporated into, or cross-referenced by, each AI vendor agreement. The SLA requirements below represent Zava's minimum acceptable standards; deal teams should seek enhanced SLAs for high-ACV engagements or mission-critical deployments (such as underwriting-pipeline integrations). The SLA terms set forth in this template should be included in the agreement as an exhibit or schedule, and the agreement should include a cross-reference confirming that the SLA is an integral part of the agreement.
A.1 Uptime Commitment
Minimum Uptime Target: 99.5% monthly availability, measured on a calendar-month basis.
Availability Definition: The Platform is "Available" when it is accessible and functioning in accordance with the documentation and specifications and is capable of processing Company Data inputs and delivering Outputs/Inferences within the agreed performance parameters. The Platform is "Unavailable" when it fails to meet this standard, excluding Permitted Downtime (as defined below).
Monthly Availability Calculation:
Monthly Availability (%) = [(Total Minutes in Month - Unscheduled Downtime Minutes) / Total Minutes in Month] × 100
A.2 Service Credit Structure
Service credits are calculated as a percentage of the monthly platform fees based on the following tiered schedule:

A.3 Service Credit Cap
The maximum aggregate service credit in any calendar month is 5% of monthly platform fees. For an annual platform fee of $2,710,000 (monthly platform fee of approximately $225,833), the maximum monthly service credit is approximately $11,292. As noted in Section 8.4, this amount is a floor for negotiation; for high-ACV deals, the deal team should seek a higher credit cap (e.g., 10% of monthly fees).
Service credits are applied as a credit against the next monthly invoice. Service credits do not accumulate and may not be applied to invoices more than sixty (60) days after the month in which the credit was earned. Accrued but unused service credits must be refunded if the agreement is terminated due to chronic SLA failures.
A.4 Termination Triggers
Company may terminate the agreement without penalty and without waiving any accrued rights or remedies upon the occurrence of either of the following:
•  Vendor fails to meet the 99.0% monthly availability threshold for three (3) consecutive calendar months; or
•  Vendor fails to meet the 95.0% monthly availability threshold in any single calendar month.
A.5 Measurement and Verification
Primary Measurement: Vendor shall provide automated monitoring and reporting of Platform availability, with reports delivered to Company monthly within five (5) business days of the end of each calendar month. Reports must include minute-by-minute availability data, incident logs, root-cause analyses for any downtime exceeding fifteen (15) minutes, and a calculation of the monthly availability percentage.
Independent Verification: Company retains the right to conduct independent availability monitoring using its own tools or a third-party monitoring service. In the event of a discrepancy between Vendor's reported availability and Company's independently measured availability, the parties shall meet within five (5) business days to reconcile the data. If the discrepancy cannot be resolved, Company's independently measured availability shall control for purposes of service-credit calculation.
A.6 Permitted Downtime (Exclusions)
The following categories of downtime are excluded from the availability calculation:
•  Scheduled Maintenance: Planned maintenance windows of no more than four (4) hours per month, scheduled with at least forty-eight (48) hours' advance written notice to Company. Maintenance windows must be scheduled during off-peak hours (between 12:00 AM and 6:00 AM Eastern Time, Saturday or Sunday).
•  Force Majeure Events: Downtime caused by events beyond Vendor's reasonable control, including natural disasters, acts of war or terrorism, government actions, and widespread internet or telecommunications outages. Force majeure exclusions do not apply if the downtime is caused by Vendor's failure to implement reasonable disaster-recovery or business-continuity measures.
No other exclusions are acceptable. "Customer-caused downtime" or "third-party-caused downtime" exclusions that are broader than the categories above must be rejected or narrowly scoped.
A.7 Incident Notification
Vendor must notify Company of any material incident affecting Platform availability or performance within seventy-two (72) hours. For data-breach-specific notification requirements, see Section 3.7 of the Playbook, which requires notification within twenty-four (24) hours.
